facts.statement: The genus Canardia was named in 2013 by Prieto-Márquez, Dalla Vecchia, Gaete, and Galobart.
facts.quote: The type species Canardia garonnensis was first described and named by Albert Prieto-Márquez, Fabio M. Dalla Vecchia, Rodrigo Gaete and Àngel Galobart in 2013.

facts.statement: Canardia is a Late Cretaceous lambeosaurine dinosaur found in the Marnes d'Auzas Formation of southwestern France.
facts.quote: Canardia is an extinct genus of lambeosaurine dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous Marnes d'Auzas Formation (late Maastrichtian stage) of Haute-Garonne department, in Occitanie region, southwestern France.

facts.statement: All known fossils of Canardia belong to juvenile individuals.
facts.quote: It is only known from juvenile specimens.

facts.statement: The type locality for Canardia was discovered in 1999 by researchers from the Musée des Dinosaures d'Espéraza.
facts.quote: The type locality of Tricouté 3, near the village of Marignac-Laspeyres, was discovered in 1999 by a team of The Musée des Dinosaures d'Espéraza.

facts.statement: Before its formal description, Canardia was provisionally identified as Pararhabdodon sp. in 2003.
facts.quote: In 2003, these specimens were provisionally attributed to Pararhabdodon sp., a Spanish genus that at the time was the only known lambeosaurin in Europe.

facts.statement: A juvenile Canardia specimen with a 11.5 cm maxilla was transported by a river to marine deposits.
facts.quote: The Larcan specimen belongs to a juvenile individual (the length of the maxilla is 11.5 cm), whose remains were carried by a river to the sea.

facts.statement: Canardia's maxilla features a prominent subrectangular flange rising vertically above the rostroventral process.
facts.quote: The main feature of Canardia is the maxilla characterized by an enlarged rostrodorsal region that forms a prominent subrectangular flange that rises vertically above the rostroventral process.

facts.statement: The precise position of Canardia within the Lambeosaurinae subfamily is debated among scientists.
facts.quote: Although universally recognized as a member of the Lambeosaurinae, its precise position within the subfamily is debated.

facts.statement: It is unknown whether Canardia possessed a hollow bony crest on its skull.
facts.quote: It is not known if Canardia had a hollow bony crest on the skull like most lambeosaurines.

facts.statement: A 2021 study by Longrich and colleagues proposed a different classification for Canardia than previous studies.
facts.quote: However, a different classification was proposed in 2021 by Longrich and colleagues when describing the genus Ajnabia from Morocco.

facts.statement: Canardia likely belonged to an archaic group of lambeosaurines that used the Ibero-Armorican island as a refuge.
facts.quote: Thus, Canardia and Pararhabdodon would both belong to rather archaic groups of lambeosaurines for their time and the Ibero-Armorican island would have constituted an ultimate refuge for these ancient groups of lambeosaurines.

facts.statement: Paleontologists suggest Canardia's ancestors migrated to Europe via temporary terrestrial links between Western Asia and European islands.
facts.quote: This migration was probably carried out in several stages, firstly by temporary terrestrial links between the landmass of Western Asia and the eastern islands of the European archipelago, then between the different European islands up to the Ibero-Armorican Island.

facts.statement: Because no maxilla is preserved in the juvenile specimens, it is not possible to confirm if they belong to Canardia or another lambeosaurine.
facts.quote: No maxilla is preserved in these specimens, so it is not possible to know if this hadrosaur belongs to Canardia or to another lambeosaurine
